subject: ent
title: Tumours of the ear and cerebellopontine angle

steps.tx: Cerebellopontine angle tumours present with unilateral sensorineural deafness, tinnitus and imbalance long before mass effects betray them. **Vestibular schwannoma** forms about four fifths of angle tumours, growing from Schwann cells of the vestibular nerve in the internal meatus and expanding medially to compress trigeminal, facial and brainstem structures in that order of clinical appearance.
steps.say: Angle tumours whisper through one deaf ear years before pressing the brainstem. Most are vestibular schwannomas.

steps.tx: **Key point.** Growth is usually slow (millimetres yearly) and many small tumours in older patients never need intervention. Serial MRI surveillance with hearing preservation intent guides modern care: microsurgery (hearing preservation or translabyrinthine sacrifice approaches) and stereotactic radiosurgery compete by size, hearing status and patient preference, while facial nerve preservation is the universal surgical priority metric.
steps.say: Many angle tumours are watched with scans. Surgery or focused radiation follows growth, size and hearing: saving facial movement outranks all.

steps.tx: **Glomus tumours** (paragangliomas) arise from paraganglia along the jugular bulb (glomus jugulare) or middle ear promontory (tympanicum), causing pulsatile tinnitus synchronised with heartbeat and conductive loss, with a red retrotympanic mass blanching on pressure (Brown sign). They secrete catecholamines rarely; imaging shows moth eaten jugular foramen in jugulare disease. Embolisation plus surgery or radiotherapy treats by extent.
steps.say: Pulsatile tinnitus with red mass behind drum means glomus tumour. Jugular types eat the jugular foramen bone.

steps.tx: **Key point.** Meningiomas form the second angle tumour, arising from dura with broad base and dural tail on MRI, often preserving hearing longer relative to size. Epidermoid cysts insinuate with diffusion restriction on MRI and chemical meningitis risk if ruptured. Facial nerve schwannomas mimic vestibular ones but add facial twitch or palsy earlier.
steps.say: Dural based angle mass with tail is meningioma. Diffusion bright insinuating lesion is epidermoid.

steps.tx: **Key point.** External and middle ear malignancy is rarer: squamous carcinoma of canal or middle ear in chronically discharging ears causes pain, bleeding and facial palsy with poor prognosis needing radical resection and radiotherapy. Basal and squamous cancers of pinna follow sun exposure like skin cancers elsewhere, with perichondrial spread making cartilage resection margins important.
steps.say: Bleeding painful chronic ear with palsy may be cancer, not infection. Sun cancers of pinna need cartilage aware margins.
